title: Al-Malik Al-Nasir and His Wazir

full_text:
Sultan Al-Malik al-Nasir of Cairo was surrounded by flattering courtiers who constantly whispered accusations of embezzlement against his Grand Vizier, Fakhr al-Din. 'Sire,' whispered an envious emir, 'the vizier lives in a modest house, yet millions pass through his hands; he must be hoarding gold in secret subterranean vaults outside the city!'

Troubled by suspicion, the Sultan resolved to conduct an unexpected inspection of the vizier’s private residence at midnight, accompanied by fifty armed mamelukes.

They surrounded the modest brick house, forced open the doors, and searched every chamber.

To the Sultan's astonishment, they found no heaps of gold, no chests of rubies, and no silk tapestries. The vizier’s private room contained only a straw sleeping mat, a clay water jar, a wooden stand bearing the sacred scriptures, and an iron coffer.

'Open that iron coffer!' commanded the Sultan sternly.

The vizier unlocked the chest with a small key. Inside lay a patched woollen cloak, a shepherd’s wooden staff, and a pair of worn camel-hide sandals.

Fakhr al-Din said with quiet dignity: 'Sire, these are the garments I wore twenty years ago when I was an impoverished shepherd boy in the hills. Every morning before I enter your royal council to manage the millions of your treasury, I open this chest, look upon these sandals, and say to my soul: "Remember who you were, Fakhr al-Din; do not let the gold of the empire corrupt your clean hands!"'

Sultan Al-Malik al-Nasir covered his face with his mantle, weeping in profound shame. He embraced his vizier before all the emirs, dismissed the slanderers from his court, and gave Fakhr al-Din complete authority over the realm, learning that true integrity is incorruptible.
moral: Absolute integrity in managing the public treasury is the only armor that withstands court intrigue.
